learningObjectives.title: The synagogue as a sacred place

questions.q: The Western Wall in Jerusalem is a surviving part of which structure?
options: A retaining wall of the Second Temple mount
The outer wall of the modern Knesset
The gate of the city of Bethlehem
questions.explain: The Western Wall is the remaining section of the retaining wall that once supported the platform of the Second Temple.

questions.q: In which year was the Second Temple in Jerusalem destroyed?
questions.explain: The Romans destroyed the Second Temple in 70 CE, leaving only the Western Wall standing.

questions.q: What is the Hebrew name commonly used for the Western Wall?
questions.explain: Jews often refer to the Western Wall as the Kotel, the Hebrew word for 'wall'.

questions.q: Which city is regarded as the holiest place in Judaism?
questions.explain: Jerusalem is the holiest city in Judaism, the site of both Temples and a focus of prayer and pilgrimage.

questions.q: Why do many Jewish visitors place written notes in the cracks of the Western Wall?
options: As personal prayers to God at the holiest accessible site
To leave messages for other tourists
To mark the boundary of the Temple
To record their names for a census
questions.explain: Worshippers write prayers and place them in the Wall because it is the closest accessible point to the former Holy of Holies.

questions.q: Why is the Western Wall considered especially sacred rather than just an old wall?
options: It is the nearest surviving point to where the Temple's Holy of Holies stood
It was built by Moses himself
It contains the original Ten Commandments
It marks the birthplace of Abraham
questions.explain: Its holiness comes from its closeness to the site of the Temple sanctuary, the dwelling place of God's presence.

questions.q: In Orthodox practice, how are worshippers arranged at the Western Wall?
options: Men and women pray in separate sections
Everyone must pray in complete silence
Only rabbis are allowed to approach
Visitors pray facing away from the Wall
questions.explain: Orthodox custom divides the prayer area into separate sections for men and women.

questions.q: A Jewish family travels to Jerusalem, writes personal prayers on small pieces of paper, and tucks them into the gaps between the ancient stones. Which site are they visiting?
questions.explain: Placing written prayers in the gaps of the ancient stones is a practice associated with the Western Wall.

questions.q: On Tisha B'Av a large crowd gathers at the Western Wall to fast and mourn. What are they chiefly remembering?
options: The destruction of the Temples in Jerusalem
The founding of the first synagogue
The giving of the Torah to Moses
The building of King Solomon's palace
questions.explain: Tisha B'Av is a fast day mourning the destruction of both the First and Second Temples.

questions.q: What is the name of the Ark in a synagogue that holds the Torah scrolls?
questions.explain: The Aron Hakodesh, or Holy Ark, is the cupboard that stores the Torah scrolls.

questions.q: What is the raised platform from which the Torah is read in a synagogue called?
questions.explain: The Bimah is the raised platform used for reading the Torah to the congregation.

questions.q: What is the eternal light that burns above the Ark in a synagogue called?
questions.explain: The Ner Tamid, or eternal light, burns continually above the Ark.

questions.q: The Hebrew term 'Beit Knesset' for a synagogue translates most closely as which of the following?
questions.explain: Beit Knesset means 'house of assembly', reflecting the synagogue's role as a place of gathering.

questions.q: Why are synagogues usually built so that worshippers face a particular direction during prayer?
options: So that they face towards Jerusalem
So that they face the rising sun for warmth
So that they face away from the street
So that they face the local rabbi's home
questions.explain: Synagogues are oriented so that congregants face Jerusalem, the site of the Temple, when praying.

questions.q: What does the Ner Tamid in a synagogue symbolise?
options: God's continual presence and the light of the Temple menorah
The number of members in the congregation
The boundary of the sacred area
questions.explain: The ever-burning Ner Tamid represents God's constant presence and recalls the menorah of the Temple.

questions.q: Besides prayer, why is the synagogue described as a centre of Jewish community life?
options: It is also used for study and communal gatherings
It is the only place Jews may eat
It is where taxes are collected
It replaces the need for a home
questions.explain: The synagogue serves as a house of prayer, study and assembly, making it central to community life.

questions.q: How many adults are traditionally required to form a minyan for communal prayer?
questions.explain: A minyan, the quorum needed for certain communal prayers, requires ten adults (ten men in Orthodox tradition).

questions.q: Only nine adult members have arrived at the synagogue, so the congregation cannot begin certain communal prayers. What are they waiting to complete?
questions.explain: Some communal prayers can only start once a minyan of ten is present.

questions.q: During a service the reader climbs onto a raised central platform to chant from the Torah scroll. On which feature of the synagogue is the reader standing?
questions.explain: The Torah is read aloud from the Bimah, the raised reading platform.

questions.q: After the destruction of the Second Temple in 70 CE, why did the synagogue grow in importance?
options: It replaced the Temple as the main focus of Jewish worship and study
It became the new royal palace
It was the only building Romans allowed to stand
It housed the surviving Temple treasures
questions.explain: With no Temple for sacrifice, the synagogue became the central place for prayer, study and community worship.

questions.q: Why do sacred sites such as Jerusalem and the Western Wall remain important for Jews who live far away?
options: They provide a shared focus for identity, prayer and pilgrimage
They are the only places Jews may read the Torah
They are where all Jews are required to live
They are used only for burial
questions.explain: Sacred sites give Jews worldwide a common focus for prayer, pilgrimage and religious identity.

questions.q: Which building once stood on the Temple Mount and is central to the significance of the Western Wall?
questions.explain: The Western Wall's importance derives from its link to the Temple that once stood on the Temple Mount.

questions.q: A student explains that a place is 'sacred' because it is set apart for God and treated with special reverence. Which pair of examples best fits this idea in Judaism?
options: A sports stadium and a park
questions.explain: Jerusalem and the synagogue are both set apart for worship of God and treated with reverence, making them sacred.

specSource: Cambridge IGCSE Religious Studies (0490) syllabus; Judaism: Sacred Places & Pilgrimage
